title: At least 30 killed in attack on Yemen market, Houthis say; government blames Houthi missile
dek: The Houthis said Saudi warplanes struck the al-Hadara market in Taiz province; the Saudi-backed government said a Houthi ballistic missile hit it. Neither account has been independently verified.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
At least 30 people were killed when a market in Yemen's south-western Taiz province was hit on Friday, the Houthis said, and the two sides in the country's war blamed each other: the Iran-aligned Houthis said Saudi warplanes struck it, while the Saudi-backed government said a Houthi ballistic missile did.

The attack hit the al-Hadara market in al-Waziya district, a vegetable and food market, according to reports. Neither side's account could be independently verified, and Saudi Arabia had not commented by Friday evening India time.

## What each side says

The Houthi health ministry in Sanaa said Saudi aircraft carried out the attack and called it a "horrific crime", demanding an independent international investigation into what it called the "systematic targeting" of civilians, according to reports. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said three airstrikes hit at about 7 am local time (9:30 am IST) and that the warplanes had flown from the Khamis Mushait air base in Saudi Arabia; he did not provide evidence.

The Houthi figures varied. One official put the toll at at least 30 dead, and a ministry spokesman said eight people were wounded, reports said. Earlier, the same spokesman was quoted by the Houthi-run Saba news agency as saying 20 were killed and 10 wounded. Reports differ on which is the latest figure.

The government side gave a different account. Colonel Majed al-Nazili, a spokesman for the government's armed forces, said the Houthis had hit the market with a ballistic missile, calling it "a war crime" and urging that the group be designated a terrorist organisation, according to reports. Government-aligned authorities in Taiz said no airstrikes had been carried out in the area. The provincial media office acknowledged casualties but gave no figures. Footage on the Houthi-run al-Masirah channel showed smoke and a damaged building, reports said.

## Background: a new front

Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed this year after the UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022 broke down, and has become another front in the wider war between Iran and the US and Israel. The Houthis fire missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia almost daily, according to reports; in October a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. On Thursday Saudi Arabia issued danger alerts at Yanbu, its Red Sea oil port.

The Yemeni government launched an offensive it calls "Operation Dawn of Yemen" on 5 October to retake Houthi-held territory. The Houthis control much of Taiz province, but the city of Taiz is held by the government and has been under Houthi siege for about a month, reports said; the UN has repeatedly warned of a humanitarian catastrophe there. On Friday government forces said they had recaptured several villages and areas in the province, including al-Nidani and parts of Sanamat district. The Houthis advanced on Taiz in September after taking the Red Sea port of Mokha.

Al-Waziya and its mountains overlook Yemen's western Red Sea coast, and the Saudi-led coalition has attacked the area daily, a reporter in Sanaa said. Earlier mass-casualty strikes in this war have also been disputed: a Houthi missile strike on a military camp in Shabwa last month killed at least 75 soldiers, and coalition strikes on a prison in al-Jawf in September killed at least 23, according to reports.

## Why it matters for India

The fighting is along the approaches to the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the southern entrance to the Red Sea through which ships travel between Asia and Europe via the Suez Canal. With the Strait of Hormuz restricted by Iran, Saudi Arabia is shipping much of its crude from Yanbu on the Red Sea, and India, which imports most of its oil, depends on both routes. Any widening of the Yemen war raises the risk to that shipping and to freight and insurance costs.

## What happens next

The Houthis have called for an international inquiry; no UN statement on the market attack had been reported by Friday evening. The government's offensive in Taiz is continuing, and fighting on the Sabr front was reported on Friday.
